title: Cut down the forest (280–289)
hookLine: cut down the whole forest of desire, not just one tree; death sweeps off the distracted like a flood a sleeping village
last: ALL CREATED THINGS — ALL THINGS PASS.

cards: You decide to quit one thing. Say it's the late-night snack. You keep the promise for a week, and you feel strong.
Then you notice you're scrolling until one in the morning instead. Or buying things you don't need. The snack was gone, but whatever wanted the snack just found another door.
Anyone who has tried to change a habit knows this game of whack-a-mole. Today's verses name it with a picture that is also a pun.

teach.h: ROUSE YOURSELF: THE PATH WON'T WALK ITSELF.
teach.b: Verses two hundred eighty to two hundred eighty-nine close the chapter on the way. They open with a warning about the young and strong who never get around to rousing themselves: the path doesn't walk itself.

Then verse two hundred eighty-three, in Max Müller's English: "Cut down the whole forest (of lust), not a tree only!" The bracket, of lust, is Müller's own, added to show what the forest stands for. Here's the pun.

In Pali, vana means a forest, and vana also means desire, longing. So the Buddha is saying: cut down the vana, the forest and the wanting both. Chop down the snack tree, and the forest simply grows another one next to it.
When you've cleared both the forest and the undergrowth, the verse goes on, you are free of the woods. The next verses show how deep the roots go.
As long as desire is not cut, the mind stays tied, the text says, like a calf that won't leave its mother's side. Then comes the sharpest picture in the chapter.

teach.h: THE FLOOD AND THE SLEEPING VILLAGE.
teach.b: A man, proud of his children and his herds, with his mind on everything else, is carried off by death the way a flood carries off a sleeping village. In the night, while everyone dreams.
One way to read it: desire keeps us from noticing time.
Sons and fathers and relatives can't shelter anyone from it, the text goes on, and so the wise person, seeing this, clears the road now. Cutting one tree is still worth doing.
But the aim is to look past the tree to the forest, the wanting underneath, and to start while the village is still awake.

how: Teachers in many Buddhist traditions quote the forest verse when explaining that practice aims at craving itself, not only at its separate outlets.

o: an axe used for clearing the woods
a forest, and also desire or longing
a vow to give up one bad habit for good

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: not enough: cut the whole forest
tied to its mother, like the mind to desire

s: the forest verse is built on a play on words
in Pali, vana means both forest and desire.
the verses say giving up one habit is pointless
cutting a tree is still worth it; the aim is to see the forest behind it.
in the verses, family can shelter someone from death
the text says sons, fathers and relatives cannot shelter anyone when death comes.

games.q: you quit one habit, and the same restlessness shows up in a new one. what does verse 283 point you toward?
o: cut that one new tree even harder.
look at the whole forest: the wanting underneath.
give up, since desire can't be touched.
games.why: the verse says cut the whole forest of desire, not a tree only: the outlets matter less than the wanting that feeds them.

practice: Think of one small desire that came up today, a snack, a purchase, a check of the phone: just one tree.

Gently look behind it for the wanting underneath, boredom maybe, or tiredness, or wanting to feel a little better, and name it quietly without fighting it. Then let the naming go and come back to the breath, in and out.

wordCard.voice: Vana. Pali for forest, and also desire: cut the whole wanting, not one tree.

orig.note: Pali vana: a forest, and also desire; verse 283 plays on both.

carryVoice: Your line: cut the forest. The whole wood, not one tree. On to the next chapter.

sources.work: The Dhammapada (Sacred Books of the East, vol. 10)
